15664-pepper-salt-or-seasoning-for-young:
Howard Pyle prepared this book of stories, poems, and pictures for young folk, first published in 1885 and reissued in 1913 by Harper and Brothers, with a special edition by E. M. Hale of Eau Claire, Wisconsin. A front picture shows a man in cap and motley stopping along life's stony path to make children laugh. The title promises seasoning: sharp, funny tales to flavor a child's reading.

Contents open with the skillful huntsman, a foolish old woman's song, a newspaper puff, and three fortunes. Claus and his wonderful staff, Dame Margery Twist seeing more than was good for her, and clever Peter and the two bottles follow. Hans Heckelmann's luck closes the set. Pyle, who also illustrated the book, mixes fairy tale, nonsense verse, and moral wit in a classic children's miscellany.
18193-ways-of-wood-folk:
William J. Long wrote this 1899 nature book, first series, published at Boston in 1902. Long dedicates it to Plato, the owl who looks over his shoulder as he writes. His preface argues that no two crows, chickens, or foxes are quite alike, and that patient watching finds as much individual character among wild creatures as among people.

Chapters follow fox ways, a merganser, queer ways of Br'er Rabbit, a wild duck, an oriole's nest, crow ways, moose calling, and Mooween the bear. A temperance lesson for hornets and a Christmas carol add humor. Readers get woodland life told by a watcher who knew his animals by face, and who asks readers to look at the first creature they meet as a stranger worth study.
18790-the-insect-folk:
Margaret Warner Morley wrote and drew this 1903 nature book for children, published by Ginn in Boston. It invites young readers to watch insects alive outdoors rather than only read about them, and it gives plain rules for keeping a captive insect kindly for a day or two.

Chapters move from dragonflies and mayflies at a pond to grasshoppers, katydids, and crickets in the fields, then to water bugs, cicadas, aphids, and the ant lion. Each section describes how the creature looks, moves, and feeds, with a glossary to help with hard names. The book's lesson is simple and steady: close watching teaches more than any page alone, and living things deserve quick, kind handling.
2302-poor-folk:
Fyodor Dostoyevsky's first novel takes the form of letters between a poor clerk, Makar Devushkin, and the young seamstress Varvara, whom he loves from a respectful distance. Poor Folk follows their small economies, humiliations, and hopes in St. Petersburg, where a kopeck can mean dinner or disgrace. The letters grow tender and desperate by turns.

The novel announced a major talent: its clerk anticipates the underground men of later Dostoyevsky, and its compassion for the poor never curdles into pity. Short and deeply felt, it reads as both a love story and a social document. Newcomers to Dostoyevsky can begin here with profit.
2353-tea-table-talk:
Jerome K. Jerome gathers a circle of friends around the tea table for a series of witty talks on marriage, women, work, and modern life. Tea-Table Talk lets its speakers argue, flirt, and philosophize in turn, with Jerome's humor softening every debate. The 1903 volume includes illustrations that catch the Edwardian drawing room at ease.

The talks are light but not empty: Jerome has real points to make about how men and women misunderstand each other. The book reads like an evening of good conversation. Fans of Jerome's essayistic side will enjoy it.
25025-the-story-of-silk:
Sara Ware Bassett's Story of Silk, published by Penn in 1925 and illustrated by Hattie Longstreet Price, joins her series on wool, leather, iron, glass, sugar, and porcelain. Dedicated to the boys and girls of Auburndale, Massachusetts, it follows the Bretton family through the silk house, Père Benedict, a supper party, the silkworms, busy days, and the silk harvest. Pierre makes a friend, Henri makes a suggestion, and the awakening of the chrysalis leads to journeys, homecoming, and Pierre as teacher.

The book explains the spinning itself. A compact cocoon takes three or four days, and worms poise on their lower bodies, guiding the thread with their front legs in wavy, irregular motion until the egg-shaped ball is finished. Double cocoons, where two worms spin together, must be sorted out, since their silk cannot be wound easily. Bassett turns industry into story without losing the facts.
29356-such-blooming-talk:
L. Major Reynolds wrote this humorous science fiction story about Henderson and his flowers. A bit of levity never hurt anyone, the magazine says, not even an editor, writer, or reader, and a laugh can lighten a load and even change history. Reynolds offers a brief glimpse of a startled scientist and his astonishing creations.

Henderson's lovely flowers promised him fame, until his flowers walked and talked too much. A doorbell cuts into his concentration as he watches a tiny green thing on his laboratory table, sliding a hand toward a switch without moving his eyes. Readers get a light, brief tale of a creation that outgrows its creator, told for a chuckle rather than a chill.
34482-the-rosery-folk:
Volume one of The Rosery Folk opens in the garden of Sir James Scarlett, where trouble starts over missing grapes. The old gardener John Monnick stands bent over his spade, denying that he stole fruit he tended through the cold weather. His mistress speaks for him while Sir James presses the charge.

Monnick admits he once gave in to temptation and took something, and says the lesson stayed with him. He describes guarding even a gooseberry against others in the household. The scene sets a household mystery in a country garden, with class, honesty, and old loyalty all in play from the first pages.
35079-the-rustle-of-silk:
Cosmo Hamilton wrote The Rustle of Silk, copyrighted in 1922 and reprinted three times by July of that year. A frontispiece shows Betty Compson and Conway Tearle, the film's stars. The novel runs in eight parts. Part one opens at Marble Arch.

A man has followed her from Marble Arch, not a sensual old man without respect, but one who answers to emotion as an artist, still young and still interested. He saw her step down from a motor omnibus and caught his breath at her disturbing femininity. She passed like a sunbeam, and he turned and followed, as other men's heads turned too. Readers get a bestselling romance of pursuit, issued with its film tie-in on the cover.
35954-the-handbook-to-the-rivers-and-bro:
G Christopher Davies wrote a Handbook to the Rivers and Broads of Norfolk and Suffolk, in Jarrold Holiday Series, here a revised and enlarged eighteenth edition. Jarrold and Sons issued the guide from London and Norwich, with branches at Great Yarmouth and Cromer. Davies had earlier written Norfolk Broads and Rivers and The Swan and Her Crew. A Wroxham Broad view faces the title page. Sixteen chapters and a full appendix fill the book.

An introduction leads into The Broad District, then Down the Yare from Norwich to Reedham. Reedham to Yarmouth, Yarmouth to Acle, and Acle to Wroxham follow the rivers. Wroxham Broad, the Ant to Barton and Stalham, and Womack Broad fill the middle. Hickling Broad, Horsey Mere, and the Waveney to Beccles close the tour. The appendix gives railway access, river distances, tides, and fishing notes on roach and bream. Boaters get a classic Broads guide.
37110-frontier-folk:
George Booth wrote a sketch of frontier folk, first printed in a review in July 1880 and reissued at New York that year. Booth asks what the words frontier and frontier folk mean now that settlers dot all the far lands. The line is less clear than it was, he says, yet the phrase still holds its sense.

Frontier life, to Booth, is not the safe farm colony with good titles and a settled town. It is the rim by native reserves, where camps spring up like a gourd in a night and wither in a day. Folk judge a man fast there and ask little of his past, since wild force can serve a new land.
37127-lives-of-the-fur-folk:
Haviland's animal lives, drawn by Caldwell, were published by Longmans, Green and Company in London in 1910. Four creatures carry the book, each followed from youth through the dangers of the countryside.

Redpad the fox comes first, in chapters from The Spring Rains and First Blood to How the Debt Was Paid and The Sheep Slayer. Fluff-Button the rabbit and Grimalkin the cat have their lives told next, and Stubbs the badger closes the volume. The fox story opens with Vix, who finds a warm old drain under the gate of the Plantation Field and bears her four cubs there in March. The country folk also listen for the rail, the strange sound heard at night before a storm.
38726-index-to-kindergarten-songs-includ:
Index to Kindergarten Songs is a reference index by Margery Closey Quigley, librarian of the Divoll Branch of the Saint Louis Public Library, with help from the library staff. The American Library Association published it at Chicago in 1914. It indexes kindergarten songs, singing games, and folk songs across the songbooks in use.

The plan is explained at the front. Three types of books are indexed: those with kindergarten songs only, those mixing kindergarten and folk songs, and those with folk songs only. The collections come from lists recommended by the kindergarten normal department. A key of abbreviations and a list of collections indexed precede the index itself. Lists of songs for special days close the book. For a kindergarten teacher with a schoolroom piano, this index was the finding tool: the song wanted, and every book that held it, in one lookup.
41880-wild-folk:
Samuel Scoville published Wild Folk in Boston in 1922, with illustrations by Charles Livingston Bull and Carton Moorepark. Scoville, author of Everyday Adventures, dedicated the book to his son, who had learned to know and love many lesser brethren of earth, air, and water.

Ten chapters carry animal names and nicknames: The Cleanlys, Blackbear, The Seventh Sleeper, High Sky, The Little People, Blackcat, Little Death, Blackcross, and Sea Otter. Plates show a bull moose, a fox family, and the pincushion of the woods. Readers get nature stories told animal by animal, in the warm style of the period's outdoor writing for general readers.
43129-the-laurel-walk:
Mrs Molesworth wrote The Laurel Walk, issued by Drexel Biddle at Philadelphia in an edition dated 1899, with pictures by J Steeple Davis. Chapter one, A Rainy Evening, opens at a smart chemist's shop in Craig Bay. Plate-glass windows and coloured jars mark the shop as part of a new order.

Craig Bay is far from a town, not even a big village, and its old shops were simple holes reached by steps down. The chemist's rose first as the place gained fame for bracing air where sea and hill winds mingle. A winter season failed, since the place is out of the way and its mildness unsure. The chemist's stays open all year, selling note-paper and even books.
46702-rhymes-for-the-young-folk:
Rhymes for the Young Folk, by William Allingham, is a small book of verse for children with rich pictures. Helen Allingham, Kate Greenaway, Caroline Paterson, and Harry Furniss drew for it. Edmund Evans engraved and printed the plates. Cassell issued the book at London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne.

The dedication is to Gerald, Eva, and little Henry, and others like them. Green hills, blue mountains, rocks and streams open the world of the rhymes. Birds and woodlands fill the promise of the first page shown. Allingham was an Irish poet with a light hand for song. Here he writes down to the nursery without writing thin. Greenaway and her peers made the book a treasure of the picture book age.
48828-cunnie-rabbit-mr-spider-and-the-ot:
Florence Cronise and Henry Ward gathered these West African folk tales, printed in London and New York in 1903 with pictures by Gerald Sichel. The title names the lead tricksters: Cunnie Rabbit, Mr Spider, and the other animals, called beef in the talk of the region. Chapters group the tales by the hour or place of their telling.

The contents run long and lively. Mr Spider wins a wife, makes a clever trade, and finds a wax girl, while Mr Turtle makes a riding-horse of Mr Leopard. Cunning Rabbit digs a well and becomes a king. Later tales explain why Mr Spider's waist is small, and the book closes among harvest-home tales in Temne-land and a ghost story.
50938-sign-talk:
Ernest Thompson Seton published Sign Talk in 1918 as a universal signal code needing no apparatus, meant for the army, the navy, camping, hunting, and daily life. Seton, chief of the Woodcraft League of America, drew its seven hundred illustrations himself. General Hugh Scott helped prepare it.

The code holds 1,725 signs in all. Its core is the gesture language of the Cheyenne Indians, with signs from other tribes, from deaf codes in Europe and America, and from policemen, firemen, railroad men, and school children. French and German equivalents are added. Readers get a full dictionary of talking with the hands.
51616-sales-talk:
Sales Talk is a science fiction story by Con Blomberg, taken from Galaxy Science Fiction for December 1959, with art by Morrow. A blurb says that to live different and exciting lives, all the hero had to do was sign, and give up his own life.

Mr Gaines watches two men cross the court toward his building. The taller, with yellow hair, carries a flat, costly briefcase. The other carries the large square box that holds the Sim. They look like door to door salesmen, and that is what they are, though called Electro Medical Consultants. Their hats look new, and so do their shoes. The yellow haired man sticks out a neat, manly hand and beams. They even know which chair is Gaines favorite. Space tale fans get a smooth pitch with a chilling price.
51771-the-trail-of-the-elk:
A tale from the Norwegian of Fonhus came out at London in 1922, with drawings by Harry Rountree. Its hero is Rauten, a wizard elk. He was a human being in animal guise, the first page says. The tale opens in Ré Valley, a long flat gap between mountains.

A slow river creeps north through red sand and bog land. Tall sedge bristles on the banks in calm weather. Cranes stride the marshes, at peace with the present hour. An old mountain farm rots there with its fence down. Bears once made the place too hot to hold, and in spring the whole valley seethes with life, wings, claws and teeth under a purple moon.
53735-the-daring-twins-a-story-for-young:
The Daring Twins is a youth tale by Baum, out in nineteen eleven. A Reilly and Britton house of Chicago holds that right claim in full. Batchelder drew the cuts, and its front plate shows a small dam vote. Front ads list the Aunt Jane set by Edith Van Dyne at sixty cents. Part one brings in the Darings in the scheme of the book at front.

Phil talks with a law man and Becky gets known in next part ranks. Phoebe hid truth, a match game, and job hunt fill mid scheme parts. Cousin Judith comes, and pact of take in papers stand in rank there. A sad talk, rules set, and a full fight crowd the scheme more. Boat race, in the toils, and a mark on cloth close its part names.
54529-phoebe-daring-a-story-for-young-fo:
Frank Baum's Phoebe Daring, a story for young folk in the Daring Twins series, was published by Reilly and Britton at Chicago in 1912. Joseph Pierre Nuyttens drew the pictures. Twenty-six chapters all begin How: how Toby Clark lost his job, how Mrs Ritchie demanded her property, and how Phoebe played detective. How the marching club was organized, and how Toby won his heritage, come later. Toby was clerk to Judge Ferguson, whose sudden death leaves him jobless, moneyless, and accused over a missing box.

The Daring children refuse to abandon him. Phoebe organizes a conspiracy of three to help Toby without his suspecting it, interviews the lawyer, surprises a secret, and telegraphs the governor. The frontispiece shows her defending the helpless against a crowd. Baum, author of the Oz books, writes small-town mystery in a brisk, plotting vein.
61754-the-masterfolk:
Haldane Macfall wrote The Masterfolk, a novel issued by William Heinemann in London in nineteen hundred three. The subtitle promises to untie the strange case of Lord Wyntwarde and Betty Modeyne. Macfall gave the book to George Meredith with high praise. Long chapter titles joke and hint as they go.

Master Oliver leads the tale, with a keen eye and a taste for horseplay. Betty Modeyne wins hearts as the tale runs on. Chapters sort fame from true worth and pride from grit. Stucco fronts, one title warns, can hide gnawing secrets. A poet who gives himself up is spurned by the gods. The style is arch and playful from the first page to the last.
63992-the-real-fairy-folk:
Louise Jamison wrote this nature book for children, and Gleeson illustrated it for Doubleday, Page in 1912. Its conceit is in the title: the real fairy folk are the small creatures of field and brook. Ruth climbs to her perch in the old willow tree with her doll Belinda, on a hot August morning, and the conversations begin. A big green and brown frog lands at her feet and introduces his family name, Rana.

Ruth hears about the wonderful spinners, the spiders, and about water babies. She goes to a concert of grasshoppers and meets the tumble bug and the ant-lion in his pit. Ants who keep slaves and ants who carry leaf parasols get a chapter of talk. The honey makers and the moon moth, the Luna, come near the end. A final chapter, Real Fairies, gathers the lesson: the marvels were alive and near all along.
64334-sales-talk:
H F Cente wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Planet Stories in July 1953. Big Bill Bennett sells sewing machines for Always-Stitch and has just come back from the Moon. He tells his boss he is quitting, since he has inherited a time machine. His late uncle left money to others and the machine to him.

Bennett plans to go some two million years ahead with Molly and the foxes. He claims the planets are arsenals and Earth may be blown off the map. Cente uses a salesman's patter to frame a flight from a feared war. The tale mixes office humor with time travel.
64715-palm-sunday-or-little-mary-s-satur:
Palm Sunday, or Little Mary's Saturday's Walk is a children's tale by Lady Callcott, printed at Kensington in 1840. It sold for one shilling, for the benefit of the Kensington schools in Peel Street, Hope Terrace, and the Potteries. The story opens on a Saturday afternoon. Lumley calls his little girl to put on her bonnet and thick shoes for a walk to Davies's cottage.

Mary carries a basket with work for Jane and jelly for her grandmother. The lane is clean, and even the rickety stepping-stone stands out of water. It is one of the first fine afternoons that spring, after a hard winter with no fine Saturdays in February. Violets without brown edges and early flowers mark the walk's holy-day lesson.
65364-pies-made-with-pet-evaporated-milk:
Pies Made with Pet Evaporated Milk is a recipe booklet built around one branded ingredient. Its contents open with the groundwork: tender flaky pastry, tips on baking perfect pastry, a graham cracker crust, meringue, and whipped topping. Only then do the pies begin, arranged by kind rather than by fruit.

Cream pies include banana cream, chocolate cream, coconut cream, and creamy peach. Chiffon pies run to lemon, lime, butterscotch, and strawberry, and custards to caramel, coconut, and plain. Pumpkin, sweet potato, pecan, and a Royal Mince pie close the list. The introduction explains the method: Pet Milk is homogenized milk concentrated to double richness, so it can stand in for whipping cream in chiffons at lower cost. Such booklets taught brand loyalty one recipe at a time.
66061-the-story-of-milk:
Johan D Frederiksen, a graduate of the Royal Danish Agricultural College, wrote The Story of Milk for Macmillan at New York in 1919. He managed Chr Hansen's Laboratory at Little Falls, New York, makers of dairy preparations. A plate shows a well kept creamery with attractive surroundings.

Chapter one treats production, composition, and traits of milk: dairy cattle, milk breeds, feed, barns, and milking. Tests follow, from the Babcock test to the lactometer and acidity tests. Ferments, enzymes, and bacteria get sections, with lactic acid bacilli named. Cleanliness, heat, cooling, and disinfectants control the germs. Pasteurization and pure culture starters close the chapter. Chapter two turns to milk supply, tuberculosis, certified milk, and city delivery.
69434-herder-s-conception-of-das-volk:
Herder's Conception of Das Volk is a thesis by Georgiana Simpson, given to the Graduate Schools of the University of Chicago in 1921. Simpson sought the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in the Department of Germanics. The study grew from talks in the classes of Professor Schutze, to whom she gives warm thanks.

Simpson first traces the word Volk through the old Germanic tongues, where its kin meant people, tribe, or army. She then gathers what Herder meant by it in his own works and in his gathering of folk songs. Later chapters treat his Ossian and the ancient Hebrews, and close with the thought of his age.
72453-the-squire-s-young-folk:
Eleanora Stooke wrote this Christmas tale for young readers, and Partridge printed it in London. The Squire's Young Folk carries four plates, one of a boy falling through ice into black water. Stooke had written Uncle Jo's Old Coat and Tom Tufton's Loyalty.

The Coker Children open the tale at Haldon, a quarter mile from their home at Haldon Hall. Nellie and Rupert talk of calling on Mrs Wills for bread and cream. Rupert wants to go; Nellie notes the dogs are with them. Bob Wills and his first visit to the hall follow. The start of the Christmas holidays, a Christmas Eve adventure, and Christmas Day fill the short, kind book.
73009-how-animals-talk:
How Animals Talk collects William J Long's studies of birds and beasts, published by Harper and Brothers of New York and London. Charles Copeland supplied the illustrations and decorations. Long had already written School of the Woods, Northern Trails, and Brier-Patch Philosophy.

The book opens with two dogs meeting, touching noses, and holding a silent parley before hurrying off together. That small comedy set Long asking how animals pass word to each other. Chapters take up the cries of day and night, a super-sense he calls Chumfo, and what he names natural telepathy. The swarm spirit, eloquent silence, and the art of keeping still follow. Later pieces follow the trail, watch deer among larch trees and black mallards, and end with beaver work.
79487-fish-talk:
Fish Talk is a comic fishing story by Winston Marks. Its head note promises a spoof with a twist. Some fishermen are always grumbling about the one that got away, it says. Our hero has more than that to gripe about. His fish not only gets away, but shoots his mouth off about it. The tale opens on a famous river of southern Oregon.

Everybody there claims the Rogue River is lousy with salmon, steelhead, and rainbow trout, the narrator says. He grants its pretty fishing holes, only he has never been able to pick the ones the fish pick. That is why he designed a fish spotter, a rig dreamed up from his navy days with sonar and radar. Much as he enjoys fishing, he likes catching one once in a while even better, he confesses.
b09-luther-table-talk:
Table Talk gathers the sayings of Martin Luther as guests and students wrote them down at his dinner table. The words were spoken across his later years and first gathered in print in 1566, long after his death. Aurifaber and other note-takers shaped the record, and this version comes in Captain Henry Bell's 1652 English rendering, edited by Henry Morley.

At table Luther spoke freely on faith, marriage, rulers, scholars, and daily joys and griefs. The voice is warm, blunt, and often funny, far from the care of his formal books. Readers meet the man, not only the reformer. These selections remain a first door into Luther's world for many.
britannica-1911-baulk:
Baulk, or balk, is a word of Teutonic stock, meaning a ridge, a partition, or a beam, explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In farming it names the ridge left unploughed between furrows or between ploughed fields. It is also the rough strip left untilled as a boundary in the open-field system. From this sense of a strip left untouched comes the common figure of a check or a block.

Two families of meaning grow from the word. From “left untouched” comes the baulk of a horse stopping short of a jump. It also gives the baulk-line in billiards and the false move of the pitcher in baseball. From the second root sense, “beam,” comes the use of baulk for the cross or tie-beam of a roof. It also names a large log sawn to a foot square.
britannica-1911-buckingham-james-silk:
James Silk Buckingham (1786–1855) was an English author and traveller. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career in print. He was born near Falmouth on 25 August 1786. His father was a farmer, and his youth was spent at sea. After years of wandering he settled in India. In 1818 he founded the Calcutta Journal there.

His paper attacked the East India Company in plain terms. In 1823 the acting governor-general suppressed it. Buckingham was expelled from India. Parliament heard his case, and the Company paid him a pension. Back in England he started the Oriental Herald in 1824. He founded the Athenaeum in 1828, without success. He sat in parliament for Sheffield from 1832 to 1837. There he pressed for social reform. He wrote a great many books of travel. They covered Europe, America and the East. He died in London on 30 June 1855. His autobiography was left half finished.
britannica-1911-chalk:
Chalk is a soft, powdery, pure white form of limestone rock. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word to the Saxon cealc form. German uses Kalk for limestone in general and Kreide for chalk itself. Geologists later gave the name to a whole rock formation as well.

That formation gave its Latin name to the Cretaceous system of rocks. In pure form chalk is almost all calcium carbonate by share. Its grains are mostly broken shells of tiny sea life forms. Flint nodules fill some layers, while other parts turn sandy in grain. English and French schemes for splitting the chalk are compared in detail.
britannica-1911-gottschalk:
Gottschalk, who lived from about 808 to 867, was a German church thinker. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says his parents gave him to the monk's life as a child. His father was a Saxon count. He was trained at Fulda under Hrabanus Maurus. In 829 a synod at Mainz freed him from his vow. He held that the vow had been forced on him.

He then moved to Corbie and to Orbais, where he read Augustine. From that reading he took a hard doctrine. God, he taught, destines some souls to be saved and others to be damned. Augustine had stopped short of that second half. Gottschalk was made a priest in secret by a visiting bishop. He preached his doctrine in Italy until he was driven out. In 848 a synod at Mainz found him guilty of false teaching.
britannica-1911-haverhill-suffolk:
Haverhill is a market town of England. It sits in the Sudbury division of Suffolk. Part of it reaches into the Saffron Walden division of Essex. Its urban district held 4,862 people in 1901. London lies 55 miles to the south-west. The Great Eastern railway serves the town. It is also the terminus of the Colne Valley railway. St Mary's church is Perpendicular in style. Extensive restoration has altered that church.

Large manufactures occupy the town's people. Cloth and silk are woven there. Matting, bricks and boots and shoes are made. A considerable agricultural trade passes through its market. The entry is a brief gazetteer notice. It fixes the town's county position and railways. It names the church and the main trades. No history is attempted in so short a space.
britannica-1911-ipswich-suffolk:
Ipswich is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ipswich is the county town of Suffolk, England, on the Great Eastern railway. It stands on a gentle rise above the left bank of the River Gipping. There the river widens into the tidal estuary of the Orwell.

The entry sketches the inlet and the town together. The land-locked estuary runs eleven miles down to Harwich and Felixstowe. Its banks are soft, well wooded, and pretty. In the older, lower part of Ipswich stand a few prized old buildings. Sparrowe's House, built in 1567, shows ornate gabled fronts to two streets. Wolsey's Gateway of 1528 is the last remnant of the cardinal's college foundation. Readers get both the setting and the relics of a busy old port town.
britannica-1911-muschelkalk:
Muschelkalk is a geology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the middle member of the German Trias rock system. The series is made of limestone, marl, and dolomite beds. Those beds lie in order between the Bunter below and the Keuper above. The German name points to banks of fossil shells found in the rock.

Such shell banks are a marked feature in the midst of a group otherwise poor in fossils, the entry says. In its typical form the Muschelkalk is nearly confined to the German region and its near neighbours. It is found across many German districts and north into Silesia and Poland. Like rocks appear in the Alps, in Spain, and far beyond. They reach the Himalayas, China, Australia, and California.
britannica-1911-norfolk:
Norfolk, a large shire on the east coast of England, fills a land entry in the 1911 Britannica. The North Sea bounds it on the north and east sides. Its land splits in two clear parts in the text. East and mid parts form a soft waved plain with chalk downs. Rich soil and thick woods mark most of that plain.

West parts hold a slice of the flat fen lands of the realm. Drains cut that fen in a dense web of channels. The famed Norfolk Broads lie in the low mid east tract. Those shallow pools hold reeds, fish, and a host of water birds. Boats for hire crowd their banks in the warm months. Sails and race meets draw crowds to their still charm.
britannica-1911-silk:
Silk is a fibrous substance made by many insects, and this 1911 Britannica entry opens a long history of the material. Most insects spin it as a cocoon in which they rest through their great change of form. The webs and nests of spiders are silk too. But the fibres used in manufacture come only from the mulberry silk-moth of China and a few moths close to it.

The entry traces the very word through languages: the Chinese name of the worm, its Korean kin, and the Greek and Latin forms from which the French, German, and English words descend. The silk industry began in China, by native records in a very remote age. An empress, the wife of the famed emperor Huang-ti, is said to have fostered the planting of mulberry trees, the rearing of the worms, and the reeling of silk.
britannica-1911-south-norwalk:
South Norwalk, a city in Fairfield county, Connecticut, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits at the mouth of the Norwalk river, on Long Island Sound, in the township of Norwalk. It lies north east of New York by rail. Its count rose from about six thousand six hundred in nineteen hundred to near nine thousand in nineteen ten.

Rail lines, tram lines, and steam boats link it to New York. The trade and mill part hugs the river, just a few feet above it. Homes climb the ridge behind. Shore houses and rest spots line the Sound. The city has a free book house and a stone mark for its soldiers. It has a good harbour with three light houses. Trade and mill work drive town life here. The entry gives a crisp view of a small port city at work.
britannica-1911-suffolk:
Suffolk is an eastern county of England, bound north by Norfolk county. Its county entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The North Sea bounds it east, Essex south, and Cambridgeshire west. Its area is just under fifteen hundred square miles in total size.

The surface as a whole rises and falls in slight waves only. A small Fen district patch lies in the far north west corner. Low chalk hills run from Haverhill north along the west border there. The coast runs about sixty two miles, most often low and marshy. Old Lowestoft holds the most eastern point of English land on it.
britannica-1911-yarmouth-norfolk:
Great Yarmouth, a seaport and watering place in Norfolk, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands one hundred and twenty-one miles north-east of London by rail. The census of 1901 counted 51,316 people there. Part of the borough lies across the county line in Suffolk.

The town sits on a long, narrow spit of sand. The North Sea bounds it on one side, and river waters on the other. Breydon Water, fed by the Yare and Waveney, gives access to the Norfolk Broads. The old town grew along the east bank of the Yare. Its marks are the two quays and the straight lanes called rows. Those lanes number one hundred and forty-five, at right angles to the quays. Rich burgesses once lived in the rows, in panelled rooms with fine ceilings. The parish church of St Nicholas, founded in 1101, is among the largest in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-and-con:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Melk describes the abbey and congregation on an isolated rock commanding the Danube. Romans, Slavs and Magyars successively held the site, until Luitpold the Illustrious drove out the Magyars, fixed his capital there, and founded a church for secular canons.

When the canons grew lax, twelve monks from Lambach replaced them in 1089 under Abbot Sijibold, and Melk flourished on corn tithes so abundant that its folk-name was at the full bushel. Pilgrims came to St. Coloman's shrine and its relic of the Holy Cross, and a fifteenth-century reform from the Council of Constance restored observance. The entry follows Melk's growth, reform and standing among Austrian abbeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-von-:
Twelfth-century satirist Heinrich von Melk, probably a lay brother at Melk in Styria, gave the age's ascetic protest its fiercest voice. His chief poem, On the Remembrance of Death, from about 1160, opens with the depravity that drove him to write. It then turns to death's horrors set against earthly vanity, with a wife at her husband's bier and a son hearing his dead father's torments.

The poem lashes the laity, knighthood above all, without sparing disgust to shake hardened souls. A second poem, Priest's Life, also ascribed to him though uncertainly, scourges clergy while respecting their office. Together they voice the Cluniac reform's ascetic spirit against the secular world, in a conflict that shaped the eleventh and twelfth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-post-reformat:
This entry sketches only the leading Catholic Dukes of Norfolk since the Reformation, with a list of the Howard line. John, born 1430, became the first Howard duke in 1483 and died in battle in 1485. Thomas, born 1443, took the dukedom in 1514. His son Thomas, born 1473, followed in 1524. The next Thomas, born 1536, followed in 1554 and was beheaded in 1572. Thomas, born 1627, saw the dukedom restored in 1660.

The third duke, Thomas, was the eldest son of the second duke and Elizabeth Tilney. In 1495 he married Lady Anne, daughter of Edward IV. He led the vanguard at Flodden Field in 1513. Made Earl of Surrey in 1514, he opposed Wolsey with his father. The fourth duke fared worse. Held on suspicion in October 1569 and freed on submission, he kept writing to Mary Queen of Scots. He dealt with Ridolfi and Philip of Spain over an invasion. Tried for high treason in 1571, he was beheaded on 2 June 1572.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gottschalk:
Gottschalk, martyr prince of the Wends, lived revenge, conversion, kingship, and murder in one violent career. Son of Udo, prince of the Abrodites, himself a poor Christian after his father Mistiwoi renounced the faith, Gottschalk was schooled at St. Michael's, Lenzen. When a Saxon slew Udo for cruelty, the boy cast aside Christian principle, fled the monastery, and raised a Slav army across the Elbe. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Lenzen to 7 June 1066.

Thousands of Saxons fell before Duke Bernard II's forces took him prisoner and gave his lands to Ratibor. Released after years, he went to Denmark with many followers, and his later career turned toward Christian kingship among the Wends. The entry's arc runs from vengeance to rule, ending in murder at Lenzen. His feast stands on 7 June in the Brussels Carthusians' additions to Usuardus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-volk:
Wilhelm Volk, who wrote as Ludwig Clarus, was a German lawyer turned Catholic author and translator. Born at Halberstadt in 1804 to a Lutheran family, he died at Erfurt in 1869. He read law at Göttingen and Berlin, served as a junior judge and then a government councillor, and retired in 1858. Friendships in Munich with Brentano and Görres drew him to mysticism and legend, and in 1855 he entered the Catholic Church.

His conversion memoir, Simeon, traced his inner road home in three volumes. Around it stand lives of Saint Brigitta, Saint Francis de Sales, and Saint Matilda, plus translations from Augustine, Petrarch, and Saint Teresa. Surveys of Italian and medieval Spanish literature, original poems, and versions from Spanish, Italian, and Swedish complete the set. He also churned out pamphlets on the religious and political questions of his day.
nassau-where-animals-talk:
Nassau's Where Animals Talk appeared in 1914 with tales from Gabon. West African folk tales star beasts that scheme, boast, and blunder. Tortoise the trickster leads the cast of forest favorites here.

The tales teach through laughter, as elders test the young with riddles. Nassau heard them at mission fires and wrote with a fine ear. Each story keeps the snap and turn of a live telling. Forest peoples' humor and morals shine in these short, bright pieces. Readers of any age can feel the fireside warmth in the prose itself. The tales' morals land lightly, through laughter more than lecture.
pepper-salt-or-seasoning-for-young-folk: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Pepper and Salt, or Seasoning for Young Folk, the title pages and the start of the contents, with no tales visible. The title page says the book was prepared by Howard Pyle, first issued in 1885 and reissued in 1913 by Harper and Brothers. The contents begin with The Skillful Huntsman and Claus and His Wonderful Staff, with songs and short pieces between the tales.
podcast-tuckercarlson-ee_oaNQlwlk:
Tucker Carlson reports on claims that Israeli groups buy pastors and track churchgoers in the United States. The episode title calls it a long heist on the Christian church. Carlson makes the charge in his own voice, with reporting to back it.

Carlson lays out the money, the trips, and the pressure he says are used to shape what pastors preach. He names the groups he blames and the pastors he says took the deal. The episode is sure to anger backers of Israel. Listeners can hear the full charge in one place and weigh it themselves. The library keeps it as a record of the claim.
podcast-tuckercarlson-lthBJP3wMLk:
A guest billed as an ex-Freemason joins Tucker Carlson to talk about secret societies and the occult in high office. The episode title names possessed politicians and demonic rites for power. The guest speaks from his years inside a lodge.

The guest tells what he says he saw in rites and in the men who rose through them. He argues that dark faith sits close to real power in the land. Carlson draws out the tales that most shook the guest. Listeners get a dark insider claim, told in full. The library holds the talk as an archive record, without a verdict on the tales.
poor-folk:
Fyodor Dostoyevsky wrote Poor Folk as an epistolary novel, presented here in C. J. Hogarth's translation. Two poor Petersburg lodgers who can see each other's windows carry the whole story in letters. Makar Alexievitch, an aging copying clerk, and Barbara Alexievna, a young seamstress, both clinging to respectability on almost nothing. The first letter, dated April 8th, overflows with joy because Barbara has looped up her curtain exactly as Makar suggested, a signal that she is thinking of him.

The curtain becomes their telegraph: raised for good morning, lowered for good night, sparing them paper they can barely afford. Through such small devices Dostoyevsky builds a complete world of poverty, pride, and tenderness, where a new pair of boots or a borrowed rouble carries the weight of tragedy. Poor Folk was his first novel, and it made his name overnight; its heart has never stopped beating since.
tea-table-talk: Jerome K. Jerome published Tea-Table Talk in London in 1903. Hutchinson and Co. issued the book. Jerome also wrote Paul Kelver and Three Men in a Boat. Fred Pegram drew plates for the book on plate paper. The plate list gives scenes and lines from the talk. One plate asks who would be a chaperone. One line begs us not to explain away all the fine things of life. One plate asks if art does in fact lift us up.
the-insect-folk:
Margaret Warner Morley wrote and illustrated this nature book for children. Ginn and Company published it in Boston in 1903. Her earlier books include Seed-Babies and Little Wanderers. Her opening word to the children sets the method. Watching insects beats reading about them, she says. Books help, but watching teaches something new each time. Look more than you read, she tells them.

Kind practice follows the advice. Captives belong under a tumbler with air let in. They need food and a daily drop of water. Sand or water should match their home. A captive that will not eat goes free in a day or two. A harmful insect that must be killed deserves a quick death. Insects are alive and should not suffer needless pain. Morley teaches the science as a habit of attention.
ways-of-wood-folk:
William J. Long published Ways of Wood Folk, a first series of animal sketches, with Ginn and Company at Boston in 1902. He dedicated the book to Plato, the owl who looks over his shoulder as he writes and knows all about the woods. His preface attacks a lazy saying: all crows are alike. That holds, Long grants, in the dark. By daylight, the first two crows one meets differ as much as the first two men or women.

He tells of a child who knew her own chicken among twenty like him in the flock. So it is with all birds and beasts, Long argues. They know each other at once in a crowd. A patient watcher finds as many odd ways and private traits among wood folk as among people. The sketches that follow watch single crows, caribou, and other creatures as persons, not as types.
